item.research_question: How can a complex concentrated alloy be engineered to achieve ultralow wear rates across a wide temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C) by utilizing nanohierarchical architecture and composition undulation?
item.material_system: Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 (at.%) complex concentrated alloy (designated NiX) and its counterpart Ni75(AlNbTiV)25 (designated Ni3X)
item.processing_route: Mechanical alloying (MA) followed by molding via spark plasma sintering (SPS)
item.test_conditions: Sliding wear tests from room temperature to 800 °C; Vickers hardness and wear rate measurements; nanoindentation on worn tracks; SEM and TEM analysis of worn surfaces and subsurfaces
key_findings: NiX achieved an ultralow wear rate in the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C, which is 1 to 3 orders of magnitude lower than comparative bulk alloys and steels.
At room temperature, NiX exhibited a wear rate of 1.7 × 10−7 mm3/Nm with a worn track depth of ~0.32 μm, effectively eliminating abrasive wear compared to Ni3X.
At 800 °C, NiX achieved a wear rate of 9.1 × 10−7 mm3/Nm, with the worn track depth being only one-tenth that of Ni3X due to a dense, fully covering glaze layer.
The NiX matrix contains nano-coupled equiaxed grains (average size 176 nm) with hierarchical A2 nanoprecipitates (average diameter 20 nm) and composition undulations where Ni fluctuates by up to 63%.
Nanoindentation revealed that the H/E and H3/E2 ratios on the worn surface of NiX at room temperature (0.0548 and 0.0276) were significantly higher than those of Ni3X (0.0306 and 0.0054).

The subsurface of worn NiX evolved into a gradient structure with a nanocrystalline tribo-layer (~500 nm deep) and an ultra-fine grained tribo-layer (~1.5 μm deep), unlike the bimodal structure of Ni3X.
Dislocation densities in the NiX subsurface decreased with depth: 2.7 × 10^11 mm−2 in the NC layer, 6.4 × 10^10 mm−2 in the UFG layer, and 3.0 × 10^9 mm−2 at the bottom of the UFG layer.
At 800 °C, the oxygen concentration on the entire worn surface of NiX exceeded 35 at.%, forming a continuous glaze layer with a hardness of ~7.0 GPa.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that the nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation enables adaptive friction interface protection through multiple depth-dependent deformation pathways. At room temperature, the coexistence of A1 to A3 nano-coupled grains and A2 nanoprecipitates activates geometrically necessary dislocations, stacking faults (SFs), and deformation twins (DTs) to create a gradient recrystallized tribo-layer that releases frictional stress progressively and prevents strain localization. At high temperatures (≥600 °C), the high concentration of oxidation-prone elements facilitates the rapid formation of a dense, protective nanocrystalline glaze layer that minimizes adhesive and oxidative wear, while the heterostructure suppresses grain coarsening.
item.limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that the specific origin of the nanohierarchical architecture formation requires more detailed simulations and experiments to confirm.
item.future_work: The authors propose that the work provides guidance for fabricating ultra-wear-resistant alloys by exploiting multicomponent heterostructures, and suggest that the formation mechanism of the nanohierarchical architecture requires more detailed simulations and experiments to confirm.
quotes: yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C
originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates

item.research_question: How do nanohierarchical architecture and composition undulation in complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) influence high-temperature wear resistance and the formation of protective oxide layers?
item.material_system: Ni3X and NiX complex concentrated alloys (CCAs) based on Ni, Al, Nb, Ti, and V elements
item.processing_route: High-energy ball milling (300 r/min, 32 h, 5:1 ball-to-powder ratio, argon atmosphere) followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 1,050 °C for 8 min under 35 MPa pressure
item.test_conditions: Ball-on-disc tribometer, Si3N4 counterbody (Ø 6 mm), normal load 5 N, sliding speed 0.2 m/s, sliding distance 360 m, temperature range RT to 800 °C
key_findings: The Ni3X alloy forms a loose oxide layer with an outer columnar crystal (diameter ~120 nm, thickness ~317 nm) and an internal nanocrystal layer (thickness ~475 nm) at 800 °C, leading to high wear.
The NiX alloy forms a dense glaze layer with an average thickness of 393 nm at 800 °C, resulting in ultra-low wear rates.
In Ni3X, the outer oxide layer consists of NiO columnar crystals, while the internal layer contains Nb2O5, TiO2, and V2O5 nanocrystals, with visible gaps causing delamination.
In NiX, the glaze layer is enriched in Nb, Ti, and V elements and comprises nanocrystalline metallic oxides including Nb2O5, TiO2, V2O5, and NiO.
Discontinuous (Al, O)-rich nanoparticles with an average grain size of 64 nm form in the subsurface of Ni3X, whereas larger nanoparticles (175 nm) form in NiX.

The deformed tribo-layer of NiX containing alumina nanoparticles and amorphous oxides exhibits higher hardness (7.6 GPa) and elastic modulus (179 GPa) compared to the undeformed substrate (7.0 GPa and 134 GPa).
Grain coarsening in the subsurface of Ni3X increases average grain size to ~340 nm (A1) and ~152 nm (A3) within a depth of 1 μm to 3.5 μm, degrading wear resistance.
The average grain size of A1 to A3 nano-coupled grains in the worn subsurface of NiX is ~195 nm, indicating good thermal stability compared to the as-fabricated state.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that the high Ni concentration in Ni3X leads to preferential formation of NiO, which acts as a high-valent dopant increasing vacancy concentration and micro-voids, creating a loose, non-protective oxide layer prone to spallation. In contrast, NiX's balanced composition facilitates the formation of a dense, protective glaze layer rich in Nb, Ti, and V oxides. This glaze layer, combined with in-situ formed Al2O3 nanoparticles and amorphous oxides, creates a nanocomposite tribo-layer that enhances deformability, inhibits grain coarsening via solute-drag and energy dissipation, and prevents delamination.
item.limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that the specific wear response is observed in the current CCA system and suggests applicability to other systems.
item.future_work: The authors propose that the wear response found in the current CCA can be selectively applicable to other alloy systems to achieve pleasing wear resistance.
quotes: The loose oxide layer increases the wear of the Ni3X, while the dense glaze layer imparts ultra-low wear to the NiX.

The presence of visible gaps at the interface between the two oxide layers suggests that they are prone to separate from each other during sliding, thereby exacerbating delamination and spalling of the tribo-layer.
The deformed nanocomposite tribo-layer synergistically enhances the deformability of the friction interface, thus preventing delamination and spalling of the glaze layer.
